full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder, J:-These two Rules, at the instance of the convict petitioners, were issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 11.11.1991 passed by the teamed Judge of Special Tribunal No. 3 and Assistant Sessions Judge, First Court, Sylhet in Special Powers Case No. 137 of 1989 convicting the accused-petitioners under section 4(c) of Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 and sentencing them thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 5 (five) years each and also to pay a tine of Taka 3,000/= each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3 months more each should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. During investigation, the police recorded the statements of the witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Having found prima-facie case, the police submitted charge sheet against the convict-petitioner under sections 457/363/376/34 of the Penal Code read with section 4 (b) and (c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 against the convict-petitioners on 25.8.1987. 

 6. After publication of notification in the official Gazette, the Upazilla Magistrate, Balaganj, Sylhet transferred the case record to the District Magistrate, Sylhet for trial. Since the case was triable by the learned Judge of the Special Tribunal, the District Magistrate, Sylhet sent the record of the case to the Special Tribunal, Sylhet for trial on 03.5.1989. 

 7. On receipt of the record of the case, the learned Judge of the Tribunal took cognizance of the offence against the convict-petitioners under section 4(b) and (c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983. The learned Judge of the Tribunal thereafter sent the case record to the Special Tribunal No. 3, Sylhet for trial of the case. 

 9. However, the trial of the case was held in absentia. At the trial of the case, the prosecution examined as many as 6 witnesses to prove the prosecution case. After taking evidence, the learned Judge of the Tribunal, on consideration of the evidence and materials on record, convicted the convict-petitioners under section 4(b) and (c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 and sentenced them thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 5 (five) years each and to pay a fine of Taka 3,000/= each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 03 months more each. However, the convict-petitioner, namely, Rajab alias Rajab Ali voluntarily surrendered before the Tribunal on 12.4.2010 and the convict-petitioners, namely, Sajal alias Sujan Meah and Siraj alias Siraj Meals were rounded up by the police on 12.7.2003. The convict petitioners thereafter submitted an application for certified copy of the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence and other relevant papers for preferring miscellaneous case under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure before this Court. After getting the certified copy of the impugned judgment and order, the convict-petitioners approached this Court with the applications under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained these Rules. 

 10. At the very outset, Mr. Subash Chandra Saha, the learned Advocate appearing for the convict-petitioners, submits that there is no sufficient legal evidence on the record of the case to connect the convict-petitioners with the alleged offence of rape. He next submits that neither the victim nor the Doctor was examined by the prosecution. He then submits that the convict-petitioners were tried in absentia without complying with the mandatory provision of law as required under section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act. He empathically submits that the notification appeared to have been published by the Upazilla Magistrate, Balagaj, Sylhet under section 339B of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not legal and proper as because the notification was not published by the competent tribunal having jurisdiction in compliance with the requirement of law as contained in section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and as such the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Judge of the Tribunal is liable to be quashed. 

 11. On the other hand, Mr. Monjur Kader, learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the Stare, submits that there is sufficient legal evidence on the record of the case to connect the convict-petitioners with the offence of rape. He next submits that the convict-petitioners did not come before this Court with clean hands as because they fled away soon after commission of the rape. He next submits that this Court not being the Court of appeal cannot reassess the evidence on record sitting over its extraordinary jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In support of his submission, the learned Assistant Attorney General relied upon a decision in the case of Sher Ali (Md) and others Vs. The State, 46 DLR (AD) (1994) 67. 

 12. Before we take up the question for consideration as to whether the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence should be quashed or not, it will be necessary to see the extent of power, scope, principles and categories of cases in which High Court Division may invoke its power and authority under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 13. In the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury Vs. The State, 28 DLR (AD) (1976) 38, it has been spelt out that to bring a case within the purview of section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the purpose of quashing a proceeding) one of the following conditions must be fulfilled: 

 (1) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused. 

 (4) In a case where the allegations in the FAR or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence as alleged. 

 (5) The allegations against the accused although constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 Similar view on the Principles and categories of cases for quashing the proceedings was, subsequently, followed in the decision in the case of Ali Akkas Vs. Enayet Hossain and others, 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 44. 

 14. It is pertinent to note that the inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be invoked at any stage of the proceeding even after conclusion of the trial, if it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of the court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. In the case of Sher Ali (Md) and others Vs. The State, 46 DLR (AD) (1994) 67 it has been decided that the inherent power under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised to quash a proceeding or even a conviction on conclusion of a trial if the court concerned got no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any Criminal offence, or the conviction has been based on 'no evidence' or otherwise to secure ends of justice. 

 15. Reverting to the present case, it appears from close perusal of the F.I.R and the materials on the record that the sister of the victim as informant lodged an FIR against the convict-petitioners under sections 4(b) and (c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983. Admittedly, the convict-petitioners were in abscondence after commission of the offence of alleged rape. Following the submissions of charge sheet by the police, the learned Upazilla Magistrate, Balaganj, Sylhet accepted charge sheet against the convict-petitioners and made arrangement for notification in the official Gazette and newspapers in view of section 339B of the Code of Criminal Procedure directing the convict-petitioners to appear before the Court to face trial in accordance with law. However, on receipt of the record of the case and on conclusion of the trial, the learned Judge of the Special Tribunal convicted the convict petitioners under section 4(b) and (c) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 and sentenced them thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 5 (five) years each and to pay a fine of Taka 3,000/= each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 03 months more each. 

 16. In order to consider the submissions made by the learned Advocate to that effect that the trial of the case was held in absentia without complying with the mandatory provision of law as required under section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act, 1974, we have gone through the relevant law as contained in section 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. 

 In view of section 5(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the special case should be tried as per the procedure laid down by the special law and the special law would get preference to the general law. 

 20. It appears from the record of the case that though the notification was published by the learned Magistrate under section 339B of the Code of Criminal Procedure that was not done in accordance with law as required under section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Since the present case is a special case under the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983, the case was tried under the provisions of special law. As the trial was held under the provision of the Special Powers Act, the notification of the trial regarding abscondence of the accused persons should have been made by the learned Judge of Special Tribunal. 

 In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case, since the mandatory provision of law as laid down under section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act has not been complied with, the trial held in absentia by the learned Judge of the Special Tribunal appears to be illegal and the impugned judgment and order passed in aforesaid trial warrants our interference for quashment. 

 21. Generally, when any case is suffered from mistrial or trial without Jurisdiction, the question of fresh trial usually comes for consideration. In this background of the case, let us consider the facts and circumstances of the case to decide the question of sending back the case for fresh trial. 

 22. It may be mentioned that when it is found after a full trial that there was a mistrial or trial without jurisdiction, the Court of appeal before directing a fresh trial by an appropriate Court should also see whether such direction should at all be given in the facts and circumstances of a particular case. The aforesaid view finds support in the case of Asiman Begum Vs. The State, 51 DLR (AD)(1999) 18. 

 "There is no question that the Court has undoubted right to direct a retrial where there has not been a trial in accordance with law. We are of the view that having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and particularly in view of the fact that in the meantime (during pendency of appeal in this Court) the appellant has continued to suffer imprisonment, it is a fit and proper case in which the High Court Division should consider the case on merit also and then pass whatever order or orders it thinks appropriate in the interest of justice." 

 If it is found that there was no legal evidence to support the conviction, then in that case it would be wholly wrong to direct a retrial because it would then be an useless exercise. Further, the prosecution should not be given a chance to fill up its lacuna by bringing new evidence which it did not or could not produce in the first trial. 

 23. Reverting to the present case, it appears from the record of the case that the victim of the case was not examined by the prosecution to prove the allegation of alleged rape. On the other hand, the Doctor who examined the victim was also not examined by the prosecution. A reference to evidence adduced by the prosecution witnesses prompts us to hold that the prosecution could not prove the allegation of rape against the convict-petitioners. Furthermore, the convict-petitioner, namely, Rajab alias Rajab Ali voluntarily surrendered before the Tribunal after delivery of the judgment on 12.4.2010. The convict petitioners, namely, Sajal alias Md. Sujan Meah and Siraj alias Siraj Meah were arrested by the police on 12.7.2003 and they were enlarged on bail by this Court on 18.11.2003. After enlarging on bail, the convict-petitioner, namely, Sajal alias Sujan Meah died on 18.11.2008 and accordingly the proceeding against him abated. 

 In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case, we find that there is no legal evidence to support the conviction on the one hand and that the convict-petitioners suffered undergoing the sentence in part on the other hand. From the discussions made above, it is clear that the facts and circumstances of the case do not warrant any direction for fresh trial or retrial. 

 24. Having considered all aspects of the case, we find merit in this Rule. Accordingly, these two Rules are made absolute. 

 25. The impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 11.11.1991 passed by the learned Judge of Special Tribunal No. 3 and Assistant Sessions Judge, First Court, Sylhet in Special Powers Case No. 137 of 1989 is hereby quashed. 

 26. Let the convict-petitioner namely Rajab alias Rajab Ali, son of Samed Ullah be set at liberty if not wanted in connection with any other case. Let convict-petitioner, namely, Siraj alias Siraj Meals, son of Mokarram Ullah be released from his bail bond.
